tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (Proc. ACM Manag. Data 1(2), Art. 152, SIGMOD 2023) whose abstract states 1.6x-3.7x vs RE2, 3.4x-7.9x vs Boost, 3.1x to >100x vs PCRE2. Sec. 5.1 gives CPU (Xeon Platinum 8370C) and -O3, but the compiler version is not stated and 2 of 3 workloads are Microsoft-internal, so not A.

corrections.hardware: Azure Standard_E32-16ds_v5 VM: Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C @ 2.80GHz, 16 vCPUs, 256 GB RAM, 1 TB disk; single-threaded runs (paper Sec. 5.1)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++17 compiled with -O3 (paper Sec. 5.1); compiler named only in repo README as g++ >= 8.4.0, exact version not stated. Library versions: RE2 09-20-2022, PCRE2 10.40 via JPCRE2 10.32.01 with JIT, ICU4C 72.1, Boost 1.65.1
corrections.caveats: No LICENSE file (GitHub license: none), so the code is all-rights-reserved by default. Two of the three workloads (DB-X, System-Y) are Microsoft-internal production logs; only the US-Accident result (1.6x vs RE2) can be reproduced with the public original_codebase/BLARE_CODE, and the 3.7x RE2 figure comes from the proprietary DB-X workload. Numbers are single-threaded first-match-per-line extraction; exact compiler version is not stated. The ACM DL page returns HTTP 403 to fetchers, but the same paper is in the repo as BLARE.pdf. Only 9 stars and no commits since 2023-11-20.

notes: Read the full paper from BLARE.pdf in the repo (ACM DOI page 403). Abstract numbers match the record exactly; the paper also reports 61.7x for ICU on US-Accident. Metadata (no license, 9 stars, last commit 2023-11-20, stale) verified.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed paper (arXiv 2407.20479) evaluated with the independent BurntSushi/rebar suite; Fig. 5a shows geometric-mean slowdown RE# 1.48 vs rust/regex 2.54. CPU is stated (Threadripper 3960X), but engine versions and compiler/runtime flags are omitted, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper (arXiv 2407.20479) states RE# places first overall on the rebar baseline suite (27 supported benchmarks), 'over 71% faster than the next fastest engine Rust' (geometric-mean slowdown 1.48 vs 2.54; the paper itself gives 2.54/1.48 = 1.716). On the extended benchmarks (Fig. 5b) RE# is first overall (1.09 vs Hyperscan 3.77, rust/regex 29.5), 'often by several orders of magnitude'. RE# is not fastest in every category: rust/regex has lower slowdown in baseline categories 6.1.1 literal/literal-alternate (1.49 vs 1.98) and 6.1.3 (1.38 vs 1.43). Repo README separately shows RE# 37x-34,833x faster than .NET Compiled/SourceGenerated on curated rebar patterns.
corrections.hardware: Paper: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3960X 24-Core, 128 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04 Docker image (Sec. 6). README table: AMD Ryzen 7 5800X, .NET 10.0
corrections.caveats: The paper omits engine version numbers ('most recent available stable versions') and gives no compiler/runtime flags, so tier stays B. Rust regex still wins the literal/literal-alternate category. RE# uses leftmost-longest semantics: 2 of 27 baseline benchmarks gave different match results than leftmost-greedy engines, and benchmarks that need capture groups were excluded. The README's own table compares RE# only against .NET's built-in engines.

notes: Opened the arXiv PDF: the 71% figure and the 2.54/1.48 ratio are stated in the paper itself, so the 'derived from page data' label was removed. Venue POPL 2025 comes from the README's DOI link (10.1145/3704837), which I did not open. Metadata (MIT, 257 stars, last commit 2026-07-04) verified.

tier_reason: First-party cross-language benchmark (kolkov/regex-bench, by coregex's top contributor). Code and build flags are public, but hardware is only 'AMD EPYC' on a shared GitHub Actions runner with no CPU model, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Per kolkov/regex-bench README (coregex v0.12.23, FindAll, 6.0 MB input, GitHub Actions AMD EPYC): faster than Rust regex on 6 of 16 patterns: inner_literal 52x (0.26 ms vs 13.55 ms), ip 17.6x, suffix 7.7x, multiline_php 2.0x, char_class 1.4x, version 1.2x. SLOWER than Rust regex on 8 of 16: email 2.1x, uri 1.8x, literal_alt 7.4x, http_methods 2.4x, multi_literal 2.4x, alpha_digit 2.2x, word_digit 2.2x, word_repeat 3.2x. About the same on the 2 anchored patterns. Against Go stdlib regexp: 3.6x-893x on the same patterns.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.23 with default go build; Rust stable toolchain (dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable), regex crate 1.11, cargo build --release with lto = true, codegen-units = 1 (per .github/workflows/benchmark.yml and rust/Cargo.toml in kolkov/regex-bench)
corrections.caveats: kolkov/regex-bench is maintained by coregex's top contributor (kolkov), so it is a first-party benchmark despite being a separate repo. Hardware is a shared GitHub Actions runner reported only as 'AMD EPYC' (no model), and the README warns that results vary by +/-30% between runs. coregex is slower than Rust regex on 8 of 16 patterns. The widely quoted '3-3000x' headline is against Go stdlib regexp on no-match edge cases, not against Rust regex.

notes: The numbers match the README table. The record said 'slower on 7 of 16' but listed 8 patterns; the table shows 8 slower, 6 faster and 2 the same. The Rust version and build flags ARE stated in the repo (regex 1.11, release, LTO), so that caveat was corrected. Metadata (MIT, 261 stars, last commit 2026-09-06) verified.

tier_reason: Vendor blog post (Manticore CEO, Jul 2022) citing db-benchmarks.com. That suite is maintained by the same Manticore team (top contributor sanikolaev; ships Manticore nightly configs), so it is first-party, not independent. No CPU model or build flags are stated, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Manticore blog (Jul 25 2022) citing db-benchmarks.com: 4x faster than tuned Elasticsearch on the 1.7B-doc taxi test; 15x faster on the 1.1M Hacker News comments test; 22x faster on the 10M nginx-log test; 25x faster ingestion of the 1.7B-doc taxi dataset (1h08m vs 28h33m via Logstash). For direct loading of 50M random docs, the page concludes 'Manticore is 2x faster': sharded Manticore without binlog did 894,856 docs/s vs sharded Elasticsearch 416,788 docs/s (plus a 13.5 s refresh). Unsharded, default Elasticsearch was 21% faster (280,519 vs 231,742 docs/s); Manticore was 43% faster only when Elasticsearch used refresh=1 (162,614 docs/s).
corrections.hardware: 32-core server with SSD (1.7B taxi ingestion test); server with 16 physical cores plus hyper-threading (50M direct-load test); CPU model not stated on the page
corrections.caveats: First-party: the blog author is Manticore's Sergey Nikolaev, and db-benchmarks.com (github.com/db-benchmarks/db-benchmarks) is maintained by the same Manticore team, so it is not an independent suite. The page dates from July 2022 and uses Elasticsearch 7.15.2 (from the Logstash log) and Manticore 5.0.2 (the docker tag in the 50M test); the CPU model and build flags are not stated. The page's own ingestion conclusion is 2x; a 5.5x figure would pair sharded Manticore with unsharded refresh=1 Elasticsearch. Elasticsearch is Lucene-based, so this is an indirect comparison to Lucene.

notes: Downgraded B to C because db-benchmarks is Manticore's own framework (not independent). The claimed 5.5x ingestion ratio (894,856 vs 162,614) mixed sharded and unsharded configs; the page says 2x. The 4x/15x/22x/25x figures are on the page. last_commit updated to 2026-09-25.

tier_reason: Upgraded B to A. SeekStorm's public search-benchmark-game fork runs against Lucene 10.3.0-bp with code in engines/seekstorm-1.0.0 and engines/lucene-10.3.0-bp. The README states i7-13700H, Rust 1.90 and OpenJDK 21, and the Makefiles state the flags (RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release; java -XX:+UseParallelGC).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Current search-benchmark-game run (SeekStorm 1.0.0 vs Lucene 10.3.0-bp vs Tantivy 0.25; results.json in SeekStorm/search-benchmark-game), as a ratio of mean best-of-10 latency vs Lucene: intersection 1.5x-2.0x, phrase 3.1x-6.4x, union 1.3x-13.1x across the TOP_10 / COUNT / TOP_10_COUNT collectors; 115x-135x on the single 'two-phase-critic' query. The single term 'the' is 7.3x (TOP_10) and 169x (TOP_10_COUNT) faster but about 3x SLOWER than Lucene for COUNT. Against Tantivy 0.25: 2.2x-9.2x on intersection/phrase/union (derived from page data). The Dec 2023 blog (older versions) reported 4.6x-10.1x vs Lucene on all/union queries, 1.6x-1.8x on intersection, and 174.8x-734.1x on 'the'/two-phase-critic.
corrections.hardware: ThinkPad P1 Gen 6, Intel Core i7-13700H, SK hynix 2TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS (fork README). Dec 2023 blog: ThinkPad P1, 64 GB RAM, i7-13700H 2.40GHz, 2TB Hynix NVMe
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.90, RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release (SeekStorm 1.0.0, Tantivy 0.25); OpenJDK 21, java -XX:+UseParallelGC --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector (Lucene 10.3.0-bp); per fork README and engines/*/Makefile
corrections.workload: BM25 lexical search on English Wikipedia (5,032,105 docs per blog), single-threaded, best of 10 runs: 300 intersection, 300 phrase and 301 union AOL-derived queries plus the term 'the' and a two-phase-critic query, under COUNT, TOP_10 and TOP_10_COUNT collectors. Uses SeekStorm's fork of quickwit-oss/search-benchmark-game.
corrections.caveats: The harness is SeekStorm's own fork of quickwit-oss/search-benchmark-game, run by SeekStorm on one laptop. We derived the current-run multipliers from results.json as a ratio of mean best-of-10 latencies. Gains vary strongly by collector: union vs Lucene is only 1.3x for TOP_10 but 13x for TOP_10_COUNT, and SeekStorm is about 3x slower than Lucene on the 'the' COUNT query. The 100x+ figures come from single queries ('the', 'two-phase-critic'), not from general throughput. The Dec 2023 blog numbers used older, unstated engine versions.

notes: Blog numbers verified, but the record put intersection in the 4.6x-10.1x range; the blog shows 1.6x-1.8x vs Lucene for intersection. Found stronger evidence in the fork (versions, flags, CPU, results.json), so the tier is upgraded to A and claimed_speedup is re-derived from current data. Metadata (Apache-2.0, 1.9k stars, last commit 2026-09-12) verified.
